title: Area VII review: Emergencies and Accident Reporting
intro: These questions mix the three Tasks of Area VII: your emergency authority and getting help from ATC, NTSB accident and incident reporting under 49 CFR 830, and ELTs and survival. Many join two of them in one flight, from the first sign of trouble to the reports afterward.

questions.q: In cruise on flight following, smoke and flames come from under the cowling. You call MAYDAY, leave your assigned altitude without asking, and the fire goes out. You land with only a scorched cowling, and nobody is hurt. What reports does this create?
options: Tell ATC about the altitude deviation as soon as possible, and the operator notifies the NTSB immediately; written reports follow only if asked
None to the NTSB: no one was hurt, and cowling damage is not substantial damage
A written 91.3 report to the FAA within 48 hours, and NTSB Form 6120.1/2 within 10 days
Only the NTSB call; leaving an altitude in an emergency needs no word to ATC
questions.why: In-flight fire is a listed serious incident, so the operator must notify the nearest NTSB office immediately, with or without injury or damage [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]]. The tempting answer is "none": cowling damage is indeed not substantial damage [[60:882|49 CFR 830.2]], but that only means this is not an accident; the fire still needs the call. A pilot who deviates from a clearance in an emergency must tell ATC as soon as possible [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(c)]]. The 91.3 written report is due only if the Administrator asks [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(c)]], and for a listed incident the NTSB written report is filed only if the Board asks [[60:884|49 CFR 830.15]].

questions.q: Over forest, the engine quits for good. You are on VFR flight following with a discrete code, you have sent your MAYDAY, and a crash landing in the trees is coming. The AIM lists extra steps that help search and rescue. Which set fits?
options: Switch to 7700 and 121.5 MHz and repeat the MAYDAY there, since that is where rescue listens
Turn the battery master off at once to prevent fire, then switch the ELT on after the airplane stops
Ask approach to file a VFR flight plan for you, so a search starts 30 minutes after your ETA
Time permitting, add ELT status, landmarks, aircraft color, persons and emergency equipment aboard, and actuate the ELT if the installation permits
questions.why: When a crash landing is imminent, the AIM adds those message items, says to actuate the ELT if the installation permits, and, if fire risk is not a consideration, to set the radio for continuous transmission [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2c]]. Switching code and frequency is wrong: in radio contact you keep the assigned code unless told otherwise, and you change frequency only if absolutely necessary [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2a2]] [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2b]]. Turning the master off early is wrong too: the AFH says to leave it on until you no longer need electrical power for vital systems [[24:353|AFH 18-4]]. A flight plan now adds nothing; approach already has you, and loss of radar and radio without a termination notice is treated as a possible emergency [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6f1(a)]].

questions.q: You are VFR on code 1200, talking to no one, when smoke from an electrical fire fills the cabin. You want a radar facility alerted before you have found the right frequency. What does the AIM say to do with the transponder?
options: Squawk 7700 with Mode C, then establish communications with an ATC facility as soon as possible
Keep 1200 until a controller assigns a code, so you do not set off a false alarm at the radar facility
Squawk 7600 with Mode C, since you are not in radio contact with anyone, then call on any ATC frequency
Squawk 7500 with Mode C, then call on 121.5 MHz and wait for a radar controller to answer your call for help
questions.why: A pilot in distress or urgency who wants to alert a ground radar facility should squawk 7700 with Mode C and then establish communications; 7700 normally triggers an alarm at all control positions [[34:29|AIM 6-2-2]]. Keeping your code is right only while you are in radio contact with ATC; unable to establish communications right away, you squawk 7700 [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2a2]]. 7600 means a loss of two-way radio capability [[34:54|AIM 6-4-2]], and 7500 means the aircraft is being hijacked [[34:52|AIM 6-3-4]]; neither fits a fire.

questions.q: Your engine quits, and you can reach the nearest airport only by flying straight through an active restricted area without permission. You land safely with no damage or injuries, and you never talked to an ATC facility. Five weeks later the FAA asks you in writing about the deviation. What do you owe?
options: Nothing, because 91.3(b) made the deviation legal
A detailed report to the manager of an ATC facility within 48 hours
A written report of the deviation, sent to the Administrator
NTSB Form 6120.1/2, since an emergency landing makes an accident
questions.why: Operating in an active restricted area needs the permission of the using or controlling agency [[60:456|14 CFR 91.133(a)]], but in an in-flight emergency requiring immediate action the PIC may deviate from any rule of part 91 as far as needed to meet it [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(b)]]. A legal deviation still carries a duty: when the Administrator asks, the PIC sends a written report of the deviation [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(c)]]. The 48-hour report goes to an ATC facility manager only when ATC gave you priority and asks for it, and you never talked to ATC [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(d)]]. Nobody was hurt and damage limited to the engine is not substantial damage [[60:882|49 CFR 830.2]], so there was no accident [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]] and no Form 6120.1/2 [[60:884|49 CFR 830.15]].

questions.q: On a busy approach frequency, one pilot calls MAYDAY with an engine fire, a second calls PAN-PAN because he doubts his fuel endurance, and you want to ask for a routine frequency change. How does the AIM rank these calls?
options: The MAYDAY first, then the PAN-PAN, then routine calls like yours; the MAYDAY also commands radio silence on the frequency
The PAN-PAN ranks with routine calls until the pilot upgrades it to MAYDAY, and routine calls are taken in the order heard
The MAYDAY and the PAN-PAN have equal priority and are taken in the order heard, ahead of any routine call such as yours
Calls are taken in the order heard on the frequency; only a squawk of 7700 changes that order, and then only for the pilot squawking it
questions.why: Distress communications have absolute priority, and MAYDAY commands radio silence on the frequency in use. Urgency communications have priority over all others except distress, and PAN-PAN warns other stations not to interfere [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]]. Doubt about fuel endurance already puts the second pilot in at least an urgency condition [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]], so it is not a routine call. Your request waits.

questions.q: You hold no instrument rating. On flight following, low scud closes in around you, and you can no longer stay in VFR conditions. Approach offers vectors toward an airport. What does the AIM say to tell the controller?
options: Nothing yet; squawk 7700 and wait until you are out of the cloud and the situation is stable before you talk to the controller
Nothing about the weather; once ATC vectors you, keeping clear of cloud is the controller's job, not the pilot's
Request an IFR clearance, which the AIM says any pilot in difficulty should do, instrument rated or not
That you cannot continue in VFR conditions and have no instrument rating, and declare a distress condition
questions.why: If continued VFR flight is not possible, the AIM says a noninstrument rated pilot should tell the controller, say there is no instrument rating, and declare a distress condition. Requesting an IFR clearance is the step for a pilot who is instrument rated and current in an instrument equipped airplane [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1b]]. Radar guidance is advisory and the pilot stays responsible for flying safely, so keep the controller told about the weather [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]]. In radio contact you keep your assigned code unless told otherwise [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2a2]].

questions.q: At night, 45 minutes from home, the ammeter shows a discharge and the low voltage light comes on: the alternator has failed. The nearest suitable airport is 15 NM away, and your airplane has electric flaps. Which plan matches the AFH?
options: Keep everything on so you notice when the battery fades, and fly home to your own mechanic
Shed all but the most necessary equipment, notify ATC right away, ask for vectors to the nearest suitable airport, and plan a no-flap landing
Turn off every radio to save the battery and land at the nearest airport without telling anyone
Lower full flaps early, before the battery runs down, then land at the nearest airport
questions.why: The AFH steps for an expected loss of electrical power: shed all but the most necessary equipment, notify ATC immediately because any loss of electrical power is critical in a small airplane, request radar vectors to the nearest suitable airport, and expect a no-flap landing if the flaps are electric [[24:363|AFH 18-14]]. Flap motors draw far more than most equipment, and selecting them on a partly drained battery may cause an immediate total loss of power [[24:362|AFH 18-13]]. Going silent skips the call to ATC, and flying home spends battery you may need.

questions.q: Your engine fails at low altitude over wooded hills. The only open field is just beyond gliding reach unless you stretch the glide. What do the AFH and 49 CFR 830 point you toward?
options: Hold the nose up to stay airborne as long as you can, and choose a spot for the touchdown only once the airspeed has decayed to a stall
Stretch the glide to the open field, since a tree landing would be an NTSB accident and avoiding that paperwork comes first
Turn back toward the airport behind you, since a runway avoids both damage and any reports
Land in the trees under control and let the wings and fuselage bottom absorb the stop; report it if it is an accident
questions.why: The AFH names the desire to save the airplane as a hazard: typical results are turning back with too little altitude and stretching the glide to reach a more appealing field, and sometimes the airplane should be sacrificed so the occupants walk away [[24:351|AFH 18-2]]. Beyond gliding distance of a suitable open area, the pilot judges the terrain for its energy absorbing capability [[24:353|AFH 18-4]]. Wings, landing gear and the fuselage bottom are the dispensable structure that absorbs the stop, and in a tree landing both wings and the fuselage underside take the first contact [[24:351|AFH 18-2]] [[24:355|AFH 18-6]]. A tree landing with substantial damage is an accident that needs immediate notice [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]] [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]], but the report is no reason to pick a riskier landing. Holding the nose up to keep flying is one of the reluctance errors; the AFH says to lower the nose to keep flying speed [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].

questions.q: Your passenger is aboard and belted in for a flight. During engine start, a fuel leak catches fire under the cowling and the flames reach the cabin, giving her second degree burns on one hand before you both get out. The airplane damage is limited to the cowling and engine accessories. How does 49 CFR 830 classify this?
options: Not an aircraft accident, because the airplane never left the ground, so no flight had begun
A listed serious incident for in-flight fire, but not an accident, since the damage is not substantial
An aircraft accident, because a person aboard with the intention of flight got a serious injury
Neither, because second degree burns count only when they cover more than 5 percent of the body surface
questions.why: The accident window opens when anyone boards with the intention of flight and closes when all have disembarked, so an engine start with a passenger aboard is inside it, and no takeoff is needed [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]]. Second or third degree burns are a serious injury however small; the 5 percent test is a separate test for other burns [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]]. Cowling and engine accessory damage is not substantial damage [[60:882|49 CFR 830.2]], and a fire on the ground is not the listed in-flight fire [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]], so the injury alone is what makes this an accident. The operator notifies the NTSB immediately [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]].

questions.q: During a hard landing, a loose fire extinguisher severs a tendon in a passenger's hand. Two days later a surgeon repairs the tendon in an outpatient visit. The airplane needs only a new tire. What does 49 CFR 830 require of the operator?
options: Immediate notice to the NTSB, then Form 6120.1/2 within 10 days with a statement from each crewmember able to give one
Nothing, because outpatient care means the injury was not serious and the damage is only a new tire, not substantial damage
Immediate notice to the NTSB only; the written report is filed only if the Board asks, as for a listed serious incident
A written report within 10 days, but no immediate notice to the NTSB, since nobody died and no hospital stay was needed
questions.why: A severed tendon is tendon damage, a serious injury on its own with no hospital stay needed [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]]. A serious injury inside the boarding window makes an aircraft accident [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]], so the operator notifies the nearest NTSB office immediately [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]] and files Form 6120.1/2 within 10 days, with a statement from each crewmember who is physically able [[60:884|49 CFR 830.15]]. "Only if the Board asks" is the rule for a listed incident, not for an accident [[60:884|49 CFR 830.15]].

questions.q: A friend's VFR flight over the mountains is overdue. He had filed and activated a flight plan, the search has started, and the operator notified the NTSB because the airplane is believed to have crashed. Seven days later it is still missing. What does 830.15 now require?
options: A report on NTSB Form 6120.1/2, because the overdue aircraft is still missing after 7 days
Nothing until the wreckage is found, since no accident has been confirmed and no 10-day clock can start
Nothing yet; the 10-day clock for a report starts only when the wreckage is found and the NTSB is notified
A report only if an NTSB representative asks for one, as is the case for a listed serious incident
questions.why: An overdue aircraft believed to have been in an accident needs immediate notice [[60:883|49 CFR 830.5]], and the operator must file Form 6120.1/2 after 7 days if the overdue aircraft is still missing [[60:884|49 CFR 830.15]]. No wreckage is needed for that. The flight plan is what set the search going: a filed plan is the most timely and effective sign that an aircraft is overdue [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6f1(b)]], and a search starts if the pilot does not respond within half an hour after the ETA [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6g4]].

questions.q: After an engine failure you land on a rural highway. A wing hits a sign post and the main spar is cracked through, damage that adversely affects structural strength and would normally need major repair. Nobody is hurt. Cars are coming around a blind curve, and a deputy wants the airplane pulled onto the shoulder now. What does 49 CFR 830 allow?
options: Leave it exactly where it is until the NTSB takes custody, whatever the traffic, because any movement of wreckage breaks 830.10
Move it and start repairs, since no one was hurt and this is only an incident, not an accident with substantial damage
Move it to protect the public, record where it lay with sketches, notes or photos if possible, and notify the NTSB immediately
Move it only after an FAA inspector arrives and gives permission, because only the FAA may authorize moving wreckage
questions.why: Damage that adversely affects structural strength and would normally need major repair is substantial damage, so this is an accident [[60:882|49 CFR 830.2]] [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]]. The operator notifies the NTSB immediately [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]]. Wreckage may be moved before the Board takes custody only to remove trapped or injured persons, to protect the wreckage, or to protect the public from injury, and when it is moved, sketches, notes and photographs are made if possible [[60:884|49 CFR 830.10]]. The rule lists those three reasons and adds no inspector's permission; starting repairs breaks the duty to preserve the wreckage [[60:884|49 CFR 830.10]].

questions.q: You fly your N-registered single from Florida to the Bahamas with a friend. On landing at Nassau the gear collapses and your friend breaks her thigh bone. The gear is the only damage. Does 49 CFR 830 reach this event?
options: No, because 830 applies only to events inside the United States and its territories
No, because 830 covers only foreign civil aircraft, and only inside the United States
Yes, but the call waits until the airplane is back in the United States
Yes, because 830 covers civil aircraft of the United States wherever the event happens, so the operator notifies the NTSB immediately
questions.why: 830.1(a) applies the notification and reporting rules wherever the events occur when they involve civil aircraft of the United States, and to foreign civil aircraft only where the events occur in the United States, its territories or possessions [[60:880|49 CFR 830.1]]. A broken thigh bone is a fracture that is not a simple fracture of a finger, toe or nose, so it is a serious injury and the event is an aircraft accident [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]]. Gear damage alone would not be substantial damage, but the injury is enough. The operator notifies the nearest NTSB office immediately, with no wait for a return home [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]]. The first and last choices turn the rule around: the United States-only wording belongs to foreign aircraft.

questions.q: After a hard landing a passenger feels sore but fine. On day 9 she is admitted to a hospital for 4 days of tests. Doctors find no fracture, burn, internal organ injury, severe bleeding, or nerve, muscle or tendon damage. The airplane needs only a new nose wheel and tire. What applies?
options: An accident, because any hospital stay of more than 48 hours counts as a serious injury no matter when it begins after the event
Not an accident by these facts: the stay began more than 7 days after the injury, and wheel and tire damage is not substantial
A listed serious incident, so the NTSB must be called but no form is due, since a hard landing is on the 830.5 list
An accident, because any injury during a landing that damaged the airplane counts, however small the damage or the injury
questions.why: The hospital test for serious injury needs a stay of more than 48 hours that begins within 7 days from the date of the injury [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]]. Day 9 is outside that, and none of the other four tests is met. Damage to wheels and tires is not substantial damage [[60:882|49 CFR 830.2]], and nothing here is on the 830.5(a) list [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]]. Application: if a doctor later finds something on the list, such as a fracture, run the questions again.

questions.q: Today is March 30, 2026. The logbook shows the ELT was last inspected on March 3, 2025. The battery date marked on the transmitter is August 2027, and the ELT has never been used. Count 12 calendar months the way the PHAK does: from any day of a month to the last day of the same month a year later. Read that way, may you fly today under 91.207?
options: No, the inspection ran out at the end of February 2026
No, the inspection ran out on March 3, 2026, twelve months to the day
Yes, the inspection is good through March 31, 2026
No, because the last 12 months counted back from today do not include March 3, 2025
questions.why: The ELT must be inspected within 12 calendar months after the last inspection [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(d)]], and the rule does not say how to count them. The PHAK says a period of 12 calendar months runs from any day of a month to the last day of the same month the next year [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]]. Interpretation: it says this about the annual inspection, and 91.207(d) uses the same words, so the March 3, 2025 inspection is good through March 31, 2026. Counting "the last 12 months" back from today is the wording of an older checklist, not the rule [[24:40|AFH 2-3]]. The battery is fine too: its date has not passed and it has not been used for more than 1 cumulative hour [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]].

questions.q: You own a single-seat aerobatic airplane, and it has an ELT installed anyway. After a session of loops and rolls you taxi in. Which statement fits 91.207 and the AIM?
options: The ELT is required anyway, because the flight was not a training operation within 50 NM of the airport where its local flight began
Test the ELT in flight after each aerobatic session, in the first five minutes after the hour, to be sure it still works
Because the ELT is not required, a false activation needs no report to anyone, including the nearest air traffic facility
91.207 does not require an ELT in it, but listen on 121.5 MHz before shutdown, since aerobatics often set off false alarms
questions.why: The ELT rule does not apply to aircraft equipped to carry not more than one person [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)(9)]]. The AIM lists aerobatics among the causes of inadvertent activation and says to monitor 121.5 MHz before engine shutdown. If your ELT is transmitting, turn it off and notify the nearest air traffic facility [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4c]]. Airborne tests are not authorized [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4b]].

questions.q: You buy a used airplane whose 406 MHz ELT is still registered with NOAA under the previous owner's name and phone number. Why does that matter?
options: It does not; a 406 MHz alert goes straight to the nearest tower, which starts a search without checking records
406 MHz ELTs must be registered with NOAA, and the rescue center uses that contact information to check on the airplane when the ELT goes off
Registration matters only for the 12-month inspection; NOAA plays no part in alerts
Registration matters only for 121.5 MHz ELTs, because the satellites still listen on that frequency
questions.why: The FCC and TSO-C126 require 406 MHz ELTs to be registered with NOAA, which keeps the owner database and runs the U.S. part of Cospas-Sarsat [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4a2(a)]]. When a registered 406 MHz ELT goes off, NOAA passes the alert to a rescue coordination center, which can phone the owner: an airplane safe in its hangar avoids a costly search, and one in flight gets a quick search [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4a2(c)]]. The satellites stopped monitoring 121.5 MHz in 2009 [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4a2(b)]]. Application: with the old owner's details on file, that phone check reaches the wrong person.

questions.q: Your 406 MHz ELT goes off after a forced landing in a narrow canyon. The satellites have narrowed the search area, and a rescue helicopter is nearby but cannot see you. What part of the ELT helps it close in?
options: Its 243.0 MHz voice channel, which lets you talk with the helicopter crew while they search
Nothing; a 406 MHz unit sends one burst at impact and then goes quiet, leaving the crew to search visually
Its low-power 121.5 MHz homing transmitter, which aids searchers in the final phase
The satellite link, which sends the helicopter your exact position on every 406 MHz model
questions.why: 406 MHz ELTs include a low-power 121.5 MHz homing transmitter to aid searchers in the terminal search phase, after Cospas-Sarsat has narrowed the area [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4a2(c)]]. An armed ELT that feels crash forces transmits continuously for at least 48 hours [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4a2(e)]]. Only the latest 406 MHz models can be encoded with the aircraft's position [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4a2]], and an ELT is a transmitter, not a voice radio.

questions.q: A shop is installing a new fixed automatic ELT in your single and suggests mounting it behind the instrument panel so it is easy to reach. What does 91.207(b) say?
options: It must be attached so crash damage to it is unlikely, and fixed automatic types go as far aft as practicable
It must be mounted where the pilot can reach it in flight, so the shop's suggestion behind the panel is the correct choice
Any location is fine as long as a remote switch is on the panel, because the rule only covers the transmitter's approval
It must go in the baggage area, at least 10 feet behind the pilot, so it is protected from the engine compartment
questions.why: Each required ELT must be attached so that the chance of damage to it in a crash is minimized, and fixed and deployable automatic types must be attached as far aft as practicable [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(b)]]. The rule gives no distance. Reaching the ELT is what a remote switch is for: the AIM says to actuate the ELT if the installation permits [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2c]], and pilots and passengers should know how to activate it by hand [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4a2(f)]].

questions.q: Your engine runs rough over farmland, and you make a precautionary landing in a hayfield. Nobody is hurt and the airplane is undamaged, but a leaking fuel fitting must be replaced before you can fly out. You missed your flight plan ETA, your handheld radio is dead, and a search airplane circles overhead. What applies?
options: Both arms vertical, meaning pick us up, so the search can end
Lie down with arms out, the general signal for help of any kind
Both arms horizontal, for mechanical help or parts with a long delay, and call the NTSB as soon as you have a phone signal
Both arms horizontal, for mechanical help or parts with a long delay; no NTSB call is needed, but report the landing and your original destination to Flight Service when you can
questions.why: Both arms horizontal means need mechanical help or parts, long delay [[34:38|AIM FIG 6-2-6]]. Lying down with arms out asks for urgent medical help and is used only when life is at stake [[34:37|AIM FIG 6-2-3]], and both arms vertical means pick us up, plane abandoned [[34:42|AIM FIG 6-2-13]]. No death, serious injury or substantial damage means no accident [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]], and a rough engine is not on the 830.5(a) list [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]]. After landing somewhere other than your destination, report it to the nearest FSS with your original destination [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6g2]].

questions.q: Your engine fails 12 NM off the coast, too far to glide to shore. You have sent a MAYDAY to approach and can see a fishing boat within gliding reach. What do the AIM and the AFH say about the ditching?
options: Ditch well away from the boat so the airplane cannot hit it, and inflate the vests before touchdown for added flotation in case the airplane sinks quickly
Ditch near the boat; an intact airplane usually floats for at least several minutes, and life vests are inflated after you exit
Ditch near the boat, but inflate the vests in the cabin before the water reaches the doors so you float free
Glide toward the shore as long as you can and pick a spot only in the last few hundred feet before reaching the water
questions.why: If you must ditch, the AIM says to make every effort to ditch near a surface vessel, and an FAA facility may be able to get a vessel's position from a Coast Guard rescue coordination center [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2c]]. Intact wings and fuel tanks provide flotation for at least several minutes after a well-flown ditching [[24:356|AFH 18-7]]. FAA-approved life vests are inflated after exiting the aircraft [[34:166|AIM 7-6-9e]]; an inflated vest in the cabin would make getting out harder. Gliding toward a shore you cannot reach only uses up the height you need to plan the touchdown.

questions.q: On downwind at a towered airport, the tower tells you to extend for two jets. Your oil pressure is falling fast and the engine is running rough. What do 91.123 and the AIM allow?
options: You must extend as told; only a TCAS resolution advisory lets you depart from an ATC instruction in the pattern, and an engine problem does not
Declare the emergency and turn in as needed; in an emergency you may deviate from an instruction, and you tell ATC as soon as possible
Turn in without a word, then explain in a written report to the tower manager within 48 hours of the landing
Keep extending until the tower approves a change, since only IFR pilots have emergency authority over ATC instructions
questions.why: 91.123(b) bars operating contrary to an ATC instruction except in an emergency, and a pilot who deviates from a clearance or instruction in an emergency must notify ATC as soon as possible [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123]]. A failing engine is a mechanical failure, one of the distress examples the AIM gives [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]]. The emergency authority belongs to every pilot in command [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(b)]]. The 48-hour report comes only if ATC asks after giving you priority [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(d)]], and it never replaces telling ATC now.
